newsitem.title: USA: OPTIONS - Dlr/yen vols off highs on Kubo comments.
newsitem.headline: OPTIONS - Dlr/yen vols off highs on Kubo comments.

text.p: Implied volatilities for dollar/yen options came off overnight highs in the U.S. after remarks by Japanese Finance Minister Wataru Kubo that he supported a "strong" dollar but not necessarily a "stronger" dollar, dealers said.
"We're coming off a little bit on this (news)," said a U.S. bank dealer in California.
One-month dollar/yen implied volatility fell to 7.0/7.3 percent after Kubo's remarks from overnight highs around 7.5 percent. It was at around 6.7/6.9 percent late on Friday.

"The present situation that we are seeing now is something also to be welcomed by the G7 countries and that was the confirmation we had within (weekend G7 meetings)," Kubo said, addressing the Japan Society in New York. "We're talking about the strong dollar."
As for a "stronger" dollar, he said: "Well, this is not actually what was meant by the understanding."
Volatilities had shot up overnight as the spot dollar broke above its early July high of 111.20 yen towards the 111.70-area, the highest levels in more than 2-1/2 years.
"Volatilities have been picking up -- for a change of pace -- on a break to the upside," the California trader said.
Traders were generally cautious about the pickup, however, and said volatilities could easily come under pressure again if the dollar pulled back into recent ranges below 111 yen.

"It looks like a lot of stops were pulled when we finally climbed above 111.20," said Kyoko Hiramatsu, a senior dealer at Bank of Yokohama in New York. "But there's still some timidness in bidding up because volatilities tended to soften quickly each time they spiked up in recent months."
The dollar's strength squeezed premiums in yen calls over comparative yen puts. One-month 25-delta risk reversal stood at 0.1/0.3 percent, compared with 0.2/0.6 percent on Friday.
The California trader said there were a few risk reversal trades where yen puts were priced above yen calls.
"The interesting thing is...it's not so much a change in sentiment but more position-squaring," he said. "I don't know if that's going to make this whole thing keep moving as much as it has."
He added that risk reversals still favored yen calls by wider margins in the back end of the maturity curve.
Traders also cautioned that each time risk reversals flipped in favor of yen puts this year, the dollar's strength fizzled out fairly soon afterwards.
Dollar/mark implied volatilities were little changed as the dollar hesitated to break out of recent ranges and test the 1.5300 mark barrier.
One-month dollar/mark stood at 6.8/7.0 percent, up marginally from late Friday levels. One-month 25-delta dollar/mark risk reversal was around par.
